The Silk snapper (Lutjanus vivanus) attains a maximum recorded fork length of 83 centimeters [Li = 83 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger members of the Lutjanidae family in the western Atlantic. This ultimate length, exceeding that of many congeneric species such as Lutjanus synagris, reflects the species' relatively slow growth trajectory and extended reproductive lifespan. Field surveys conducted across the Caribbean shelf have consistently documented individuals approaching this asymptotic size, though such large specimens are increasingly uncommon due to fishing pressure. Newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs as yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a diminutive starting mass derived from an egg diameter of roughly 0.85 millimeters. This minimal initial mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding shortly after yolk-sac resorption, a period during which first-feeding larvae depend heavily on small copepod nauplii. The contrast between the minute neonate and the massive adult underscores the pronounced size range this species occupies across its ontogeny, spanning five orders of magnitude in wet body weight.

Sexual maturation in Silk snapper occurs when individuals reach a fork length of 41.6 centimeters [Lp = 41.6 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet body weight at puberty of approximately 952 grams [Wwp = approximately 952 grams]. This length threshold, representing roughly half the ultimate fork length, is consistent with the maturation schedule observed in other moderately long-lived tropical snappers. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals sampled along the Brazilian continental shelf indicates that vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis are well underway by the time this fork length is attained, confirming that puberty is closely tied to somatic size rather than chronological age alone. The weight at puberty, derived from the length-weight relationship for this species, suggests that females allocate substantial somatic reserves toward initial gamete production once this body mass is achieved. The onset of reproductive activity at this moderate size allows individuals to contribute to the spawning population well before reaching their maximum dimensions, a life-history strategy that buffers population resilience against exploitation of larger, older fish.

Reproductive output in Lutjanus vivanus is considerable, with adult females producing approximately 17,808 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 17,808 eggs per day] under optimal thermal conditions maintained at 21.2 °C [T = 21.2 °C] when measured at a total length of 48.5 centimeters. This daily fecundity estimate, extrapolated from fecundity data for the congener Lutjanus carponotatus and adjusted for body size differences, reflects the high reproductive potential characteristic of broadcast-spawning lutjanids. Spawning occurs in aggregations over the continental shelf edge, with females releasing batches of pelagic eggs during extended spawning seasons that may span several months. The daily rate of egg production underscores the energetic demands placed on mature females, which must sustain high feeding rates to support continuous oocyte development. Field observations of gravid individuals indicate that spawning events are synchronized with lunar cycles and local current patterns, likely enhancing egg dispersal and larval survival in the variable reef environment.

The ultimate wet weight attained by Silk snapper adults has been estimated at 7,407 grams [Wwi = 7,407 grams], based on the length-weight relationship derived from a large sample of individuals across the species' geographic range. This asymptotic body mass corresponds to the maximum recorded fork length of 83 centimeters and reflects the substantial somatic investment required to reach these upper size limits. Comparative analysis with other western Atlantic lutjanids reveals that this ultimate weight is intermediate between the smaller lane snapper (Lutjanus synagris) and the larger cubera snapper (Lutjanus cyanopterus), positioning L. vivanus as a moderately large-bodied predator on reef and shelf-edge habitats. The length-weight coefficient used in this estimation, drawn from fishery-independent surveys, shows strong agreement with values reported for conspecifics in the Gulf of Mexico. These large individuals, which may represent the oldest and most fecund segment of the population, are disproportionately important for larval recruitment and are especially vulnerable to targeted fishing pressure.

Maximum lifespan in the Silk snapper has been documented at approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years] under the average ambient temperature regime of 21.2 °C [T = 21.2 °C] characteristic of its deep reef habitat. This exceptional longevity, verified through otolith increment analysis of individuals from the Bahamas and the Caribbean, places L. vivanus among the longer-lived members of the Lutjanidae and underscores a life-history strategy centered on delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output across many decades. The oldest individuals, often exceeding 75 centimeters in fork length, continue to spawn annually, contributing substantially to the cumulative reproductive effort of the population. This extended lifespan, in combination with the moderate age at maturity inferred from the puberty length, suggests a life-history pattern that buffers against environmental stochasticity through multiple reproductive seasons. The thermal regime at depth, remaining relatively stable near 21.2 °C year-round, is thought to contribute to the slow metabolic aging observed in this species compared to more thermolabile, shallow-water lutjanids.
